concepts.definition: A polycrystalline specimen contains randomly oriented microcrystals. Those satisfying Bragg's condition diffract electrons into cones; the screen intersects these cones as rings.
concepts.when_to_use: Use to explain why rings rather than isolated spots appear.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.definition: θ is the Bragg angle to a reflecting crystal plane; the angle between the incident and diffracted beam is 2θ.
concepts.when_to_use: Do not confuse θ with the full beam-deflection angle.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.definition: In the lecture's detector geometry, the ring radius r, effective distance D and scattering angle obey a tangent relation.
concepts.when_to_use: Use the lecture diagram's definitions of r and D; if a different apparatus defines ring diameter, divide it by two first.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.definition: For small angles in radians, tan(2θ)≈2θ and sinθ≈θ. Combining detector geometry with Bragg's law yields the ring-radius relation.
concepts.when_to_use: Requires small θ and consistent distance/radius definitions.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.definition: For a measured diffraction-ring radius and known electron wavelength, Bragg's law estimates the lattice-plane spacing.
concepts.when_to_use: The diffraction order n must be identified; use the small-angle regime.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.definition: For electrons accelerated through potential U from rest, nonrelativistic momentum p≈√(2mₑeU), so wavelength and ring radius decrease with increasing voltage.
concepts.when_to_use: Assumes fixed d, D, n and nonrelativistic electron energy.

concepts.definition: For the same d and diffraction order, longer de Broglie wavelength requires a larger Bragg angle and thus a larger diffraction ring.
concepts.when_to_use: Compare the same lattice planes and order; angles must remain physically allowed.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.front: de Broglie wavelength from kinetic energy
concepts.definition: For a nonrelativistic particle, momentum p=mv=√(2mEkin), giving wavelength λ=h/p.
concepts.when_to_use: Do not use p=mv at relativistic speeds.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.definition: The slide gives an electron de Broglie wavelength in ångströms when kinetic energy is inserted in electronvolts.
concepts.when_to_use: Nonrelativistic approximation; E is electron kinetic energy.
concepts.source_status: Transcribed and explained from user-provided lecture photographs; approximations stated explicitly

concepts.definition: The slide gives a helium-atom de Broglie wavelength in ångströms when kinetic energy is inserted in millielectronvolts.
concepts.when_to_use: For helium atoms, not electrons; nonrelativistic kinetic energy.

concepts.front: Particle energy ranges for crystal diffraction
concepts.definition: The lecture compares electrons of about 10–500 eV and helium atoms of about 10–100 meV as probes with wavelengths comparable to atomic spacings.
concepts.when_to_use: Use these as the example ranges on the slide, not universal experimental limits.

concepts.definition: Record ring radii at several acceleration voltages and compare r with the de Broglie scaling predicted by Bragg diffraction.
concepts.when_to_use: Check whether r is a radius or diameter and whether nonrelativistic and small-angle approximations hold.
